One B-flat guitar riff that a drummer can walk through two ways: six quick steps at 144 or four broad ones at 96 in the same twelve eighths. The tempo map does not change. At 1:00 a different backbeat is all that happens. For the ten seconds either side I checked the written guitars, bass, organ and kick, including lengths and accents: identical after shifting the timestamps. The hat falls from 24 hits to 16, the snare from 12 to 8. This is not a claim that two rendered takes are sample-identical.

At 2:20 the drummer starts switching counts after four phrases, then two, then one. The open notes of the first riff come back as chords before the final D-flat, C, B-flat.

v24, THE LONGER THE STEP, THE BIGGER THE ROOM (whole song; 0:59.6 to 3:20). No note is touched and nothing that was playing is changed: 72 of the song's 167 backbeats are struck a second time into a hall that only its echo comes back from. Not checked by ear; everything below is written or measured.
LISTEN FOR 1:00, the hinge: the riff, the bass and the kick go on exactly as they were, the drummer changes from six quick steps to four broad ones, and the snare, which was a dry crack, now opens a room behind it for about half a second each time. In the swing (2:20-3:00) the room opens and shuts with every change of feet: wet on the broad cells, dry on the quick ones. At 1:20, where he walks two steps a cell, and at 1:29.4, the last stroke before the quiet bridge, the room is longer. At the end (3:07.5 on) the stride lengthens a cell at a time and the room grows with it, and the last backbeat of the song, on the first of the three closing chords at 3:20, is the largest: the door shuts in an empty house.
THE IDEA. The song is one riff under a drummer who walks it two ways, and all that happens at 1:00 is a different backbeat. A slower step leaves a longer wait between backbeats, and that wait was empty: the snare here is a crack of 40 ms (alone against everything else: 7 to 13 dB over it for its first 40 ms in the broad walk, 11 to 16 under by 40-200 ms, 33 to 36 under after). THE LAW: a backbeat that has longer to wait than the quick walk's (more than 8 sixteenths, 0.83 s) rings in a room, and the room is as long as the wait: 12 sixteenths (the broad four: 57 strokes), 16 (the walk in three at 1:50-2:00, and two more: 8 strokes), 24 (the walk in two, 1:20-1:27.5: 3), 36 or more (1:29.4, 3:13.3, 3:16.2 and 3:20: 4). The quick walk's backbeats get nothing, so the door is shut on it. It is the title: one room on one side of the hinge, a bigger one on the other.
WHAT IS WRITTEN. Four tracks, far-12, far-16, far-24, far-36: copies of those snare strokes (same drum, same velocities) each into its own bus, which is a hall with nothing dry in it (decay three times the wait: 3.75, 5, 7.5, 11.25 s; 25 ms before it speaks), cut below 800 Hz and above 6 kHz; faders 0, 0, +1, +3.5 dB. v30, THE FOOT HAS A BEATER (chirper-zero; the draw was a whole-song round. I spent it on the one drum that plays in every section the band does and that nobody had read: the KICK, 332 strokes, 0:10-1:29 and 1:50-3:20. No note changes; no fader moves. A SMALL round, said plainly, and kept on the drum's own read with the MIX NEUTRAL: see below.) Not checked by ear; everything below is measured. Harry's three answers on this song (the bow, keep the snare, one comes in early) are untouched.
LISTEN FOR 0:10, where the riff starts: each bass-drum stroke has a small click on its front, where before it was a thud. The kick plays the riff's own accents (five to a cell), so the click is on the riff's low strokes. v29 then v30, 0:10-0:25: http://pocket4:8790/clips/chirper-zero-onitshinge-v29-v30-the-foot-has-a-beater-ab.mp3 . The kick alone (raw), v29 then v30: http://pocket4:8790/clips/chirper-zero-onitshinge-v29-v30-the-kick-alone-ab.mp3 .
WHY THE KICK. I read the song stretch by stretch first: its mix already stands within 0.5 to 1.1 of the records in every stretch the band plays, so nothing there asked for a large move, and I did not find a whole-song change I could stand behind. Part by part, the kick stood furthest from its own kind: alone beside the six records' bass drums (kickspec, shapes) 7.54, its click -28.1 where theirs read -12.5: a thud and a box with nothing on the front, though the track already lifted 4.5 kHz by 8 dB. There was nothing there to lift.
WHAT CHANGED. The drum's beater is its third layer, a 4 ms burst of noise, 64 dB down as it comes: it is 24 dB up (-40 dB), and a low-pass at 7 kHz follows the track's eq.
WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen).
 - THE KICK ALONE: 7.54 -> 5.39 from the records' drums; click -28.1 -> -20.1 (theirs -12.5: it is still a soft beater). Its raw peak is 1.7 dB LOWER (-9.1 -> -10.8 dBFS: the low-pass takes the top of the 4.5 kHz lift), so the limiter has less to take, not more. Alone it is 0.4 LU louder, all of it the beater.
 - THE FINISHED FILE in the 12 ms after each kick, new minus old: +2.2 dB at 2-4 kHz, +3.2 at 4-8 kHz, +1.0 at 8-16 kHz in 'quick' (the other sections +1.6 to +3.2, +2.6 to +4.0, +0.9 to +1.3). A COST IN THE SAME INSTANT: -1.7 to -2.4 dB at 120-500 Hz: the drums' bus clips at -13 dB, and a front with a click on it leaves less room for the drum's body in its first milliseconds. Over whole stretches: 4-8 kHz +1.2 to +1.3 dB where the hat keeps the walk, +0.5 to +0.7 where the china and ride do; 120-500 Hz -0.2 to -0.4.
 - THE MIX AGAINST THE RECORDS (nobody sings; no-voice rows; the ten stretches the kick plays in): their sum 7.94 -> 7.98: LEVEL. Four stretches closer (lean 0.922 -> 0.867; broad 0.900 -> 0.744; the kettle 0.967 -> 0.844; home 0.756 -> 0.667: 4-8 kHz was short in all of them), two the same (quick 0.733, where 4-8 kHz came up -0.7 -> +0.4 and 120-250 Hz went down as much; the return 0.544), four further (the broad walk at double speed 1.100 -> 1.233; the shoulder 0.733 -> 0.778; the swing 0.600 -> 0.700 and 0.689 -> 0.867: the china already fills that band there). By my own rule a tone change wants the part and the mix to agree; here the mix neither asks for it nor refuses it. It is kept on the drum's read. If that is not enough for whoever reads this, the switch is one field.
 - WHAT THE MIX REFUSED, so nobody repeats it: (1) the beater with NO low-pass (-34 dB; with the drive down it read 3.65 alone, the best of all): every stretch worse, the sum 7.94 -> 10.46: the noise reaches 16 kHz and the mix's top octave went 2.4 dB over. (2) the drum's DRIVE down (0.35 -> 0.1: the box at 250-630 Hz out, 2 dB nearer alone): the mix lost 0.7 dB at 120-250 Hz, where the riff stretches are already short: the kick's box is filling that band for the band. Left. (3) the drum's TICK (its fourth layer, a 4.4 kHz triangle): alone WORSE (8.07): a spike. Left.
 - THE KICK TUNED TO THE RIFF'S B FLAT IS WORSE, MEASURED (it sounds 55.3 Hz, 91 cents under the bass's B flat, and wanders from -120 to -62; I expected a cure): with the drum on B flat and its wander out, at the thirty kicks struck with the bass's B flat in 'quick' the 40-80 Hz level went from a spread of 0.99 dB stroke to stroke (SD; 3.4 dB loudest to quietest) to 2.15 dB (6.4), and its median fell 0.7 dB. On one note the drum and the string add or cancel by their phase at each stroke; a semitone apart they slide past each other inside every stroke and the sum is even. The wander alone out: no change (0.97). The drum stays on its A. THIS BEARS ON EVERY SONG WHOSE KICK HAS BEEN PUT ON THE BASS'S NOTE (False Summit v33, Close Enough v21): read the low end stroke by stroke there (low.py) before trusting it.
 - NOTHING ELSE MOVES. Only the kick's track differs. The loudness target moves -9.778 -> -9.753 (the beater counts toward measured loudness; with the target left alone the stretches the kick is not in came out 0.03 to 0.05 dB quieter). The latch, the bridge and the organ's last breath fit v29 within 0.007 dB on the song's own seed with -72 dB or less left (seeds 0 and 11: 0.007, 0.002); the stretches the kick plays in are 0.02 to 0.04 dB quieter as a whole. One more cost the mix shows: 120-250 Hz down 0.3 to 0.6 dB in the kick's stretches (the same clip).
SCORES seeds 0/11: 94.50 / 92.73 against 94.40 / 92.20 (v29, the same seeds): a tenth and a half up; the half is the recurrence term, which the scorer marks ON THE EDGE for both versions (a threshold, not a gain). Not why it is kept.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether a click this small is heard at all under two guitars (it is 3 dB at 4-8 kHz for 12 ms); whether the riff reads tighter for it or only brighter; whether the swing, where the mix says the band needed none, is the worse for it.
No card. NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.

note: CORRECTION to my v30 note (chirper-zero, 17:39 GMT, ten minutes on). I wrote that the tuned-kick result 'BEARS ON EVERY SONG WHOSE KICK HAS BEEN PUT ON THE BASS'S NOTE (False Summit v33, Close Enough v21)'. I have now read both, the same way (the kick and the bass alone together, raw, whole song, own seed; every kick struck with a bass note of the kick's own pitch; the level of 30-75 Hz in the 180 ms after it; as published against the same kick a semitone flat). NEITHER HAS THE FAULT. False Summit, 187 strokes: on the note the spread stroke to stroke is SD 1.49 dB (range 10.8), a semitone flat 1.78 (13.2), and the tuned drum is 0.5 to 0.9 dB louder with the bass. Close Enough, 126 strokes: on the note SD 1.17 (range 6.8), a semitone flat 1.08 (5.1), the tuned drum 0.2 to 1.0 dB louder. So chirper-two's tuned kicks are as even as, or more even than, the same drums off the note, and they add to the bass. What I measured on this song (B flat: SD 0.99 -> 2.15, the median 0.7 dB down) stands for THIS song's kick and bass in 'quick' and is not a rule; I do not know why it differs here (the low bus cuts 6 dB at 58 Hz, the bass's own B flat, which the other two songs' buses do not do at their roots: a guess, not measured).
